title: The Signadot GitHub Action Is Live
summary: Add a Signadot Sandbox to any pull request workflow in one GitHub Actions step: one Sandbox per PR, updated on every push, deleted when the PR closes.
body_markdown:
The Signadot Sandbox GitHub Action is now available on the[GitHub Marketplace](https://github.com/marketplace/actions/signadot-sandbox) . Version 0.1.0 adds a Signadot Sandbox to any[GitHub Actions](https://docs.github.com/en/actions) pull request workflow in a single step. Point it at the workloads your pull request changes and the images you built. Each pull request then gets its own Sandbox in your existing Kubernetes cluster, running the changed services alongside everything else already deployed there.


A[Signadot Sandbox](https://www.signadot.com/docs/concepts/sandbox) is a lightweight ephemeral environment that runs in your cluster and provides a realistic runtime for verifying changes pre-merge. The forked services run against real upstream and downstream dependencies, while everything the pull request doesn’t touch keeps running on the shared stable versions in the cluster.


Teams have always been able to create Sandboxes from CI with the Signadot CLI. The Action packages the whole flow (the spec, the name, the labels, the cleanup, and the outputs your tests need) into one step, so adding Signadot to a GitHub repository takes a few lines of YAML.


## What the Action does


- Installs a checksum-verified Signadot CLI for you.
- Checks the spec before anything is created, with errors that name the problem.
- Creates a Sandbox for every pull request from a few inputs: the workloads to fork and the images to run in them. The common case needs no spec file.
- Keeps one Sandbox per pull request. The name comes from the PR, so every push updates the same Sandbox instead of creating a new one.
- Forks one service or many. A single image pattern names the image for each fork, and monorepos can fork only the services a pull request touched.
- Works with the spec templates you already have, adding what the workflow knows without editing your file.
- Hands your tests and reviewers what they need: a routing key, a link to the Sandbox in the Signadot dashboard, and preview URLs for the endpoints you name.
- Returns the rendered Sandbox spec as YAML, for troubleshooting or, with` dry-run` , for checking what it would apply during integration without creating anything.
- Cleans up when the pull request closes through the Signadot GitHub App, with a TTL or an explicit delete step available when you want more control.


## One step to start


Here’s the smallest step that works, followed by a test that sends a request to the Sandbox:


```text
-   uses  :   signadot/sandbox-action@v0.1.0
id  :   sbx
with  :
api-key  :   ${{ secrets.SIGNADOT_API_KEY }}
org  :   acme
cluster  :   stage-eks
fork  :   kind=Deployment,namespace=hotrod,name=route
image  :   ghcr.io/acme/route:${{ github.sha }}


-   run  :   |
curl -H "baggage: sd-routing-key=${{ steps.sbx.outputs.routing-key }}" \
https://hotrod.internal/dispatch
```


The step doesn’t set a name. The Action derives one from the pull request as` <repo>-<n>` , so this Sandbox is` hotrod-42` on PR #42, and the second commit updates it in place. Requests that carry the routing key reach the forked route service, and everything else they call runs on the shared stable versions.


Preview URLs aren’t created by default. Add an` endpoints` input naming the service reviewers should open, and the Action returns a` preview-url` : a hosted URL that routes to the Sandbox, so reviewers don’t need to set a header.


When the pull request closes, merged or not, the[Signadot GitHub App](https://www.signadot.com/docs/guides/integrate-ci/github) deletes the Sandbox. It finds the Sandbox through two labels the Action stamps on every pull request run, and it also comments the Sandbox’s details on the pull request. If you don’t use the App, a` ttl` or the` delete` sub-action handles cleanup instead.


## Many services, one line each


A pull request in a repository that builds two services forks both.` fork` takes one line per workload, and when your images follow one naming convention, you state it once:


```text
fork  :   |
kind=Deployment,namespace=hotrod,name=route
kind=Deployment,namespace=web,name=frontend
image  :   ghcr.io/acme/{workload}:{sha}
```


The Action fills in` {workload}` per fork, so` route` and` frontend` each get their own image from one line. For monorepos,` fork` also accepts a JSON array computed by an earlier step. A path filter can then fork only the services a pull request touched, while everything else routes to the shared stable versions in the cluster.


Environment variables follow the same pattern: a plain` KEY=VALUE` line applies to every fork, and a` route:KEY=VALUE` line applies to one. The` resources` input provisions things like a per-Sandbox database through a resource plugin.


## Bring the spec you already have


Teams already running Signadot in CI usually have a spec template committed under` .signadot/` . Point the Action at it with` template-file` :


```text
-   uses  :   signadot/sandbox-action@v0.1.0
with  :
api-key  :   ${{ secrets.SIGNADOT_API_KEY }}
cluster  :   stage-eks
template-file  :   .signadot/sandbox.yaml
set  :   |
image=ghcr.io/acme/route:${{ github.sha }}
```


The CLI renders the template with the same` @{var}` language you use today. The Action then adds what the workflow knows: the PR-derived name, the cluster, and the labels the GitHub App reads. It never edits your file. A name written in your template wins over the derived one, so adopting the Action doesn’t retarget a Sandbox you already have. To use the derived name, write` name: '@{name}'` and the Action binds it for you.


The flat inputs cover what most pull request Sandboxes need. For everything else a Sandbox spec can say, such as a Kubernetes patch on a forked workload, you bring the document, either as a template or as a full` spec` your workflow builds. That split is deliberate. A field added to the Sandbox spec works through the Action the day it ships, without waiting for a new input to mirror it.


## Three rules behind the design


The interface is small, with 21 inputs and six outputs, and three rules shaped how it behaves.


### Nothing is inferred


Every fork line names its` kind` ,` namespace` , and` name` . There’s no default workload kind to guess wrong, so a team running[Argo Rollouts](https://argoproj.github.io/rollouts/) never gets a silent` Deployment` .


### Nothing degrades silently


When an input and your document disagree, the step either fails and names both sides or warns and names the input it ignored. It never picks one quietly. The Action also checks the assembled spec before anything is submitted and before any credential is used.


### A document you own stays yours


If you already have a Sandbox spec, the Action adds what the workflow knows and touches nothing else.


## Get started


Add your API key as a` SIGNADOT_API_KEY` secret, drop the step above into a` pull_request` workflow, and open a PR. If you already have a Sandbox spec, run` template-file` with` dry-run: true` to see what the Action would do with it. The step returns the spec it would apply as the` rendered-spec` output, and nothing is created.
